answer.evidence: radon/complexity.py:78-94 add_inner_blocks does the flattening. It pops blocks from a worklist, and for each block's 'closures' and 'inner_classes' it makes a copy with a qualified name (block.name + '.' + i_block.name) and pushes it back. This handles nesting to any depth. Methods of a named inner class get classname=named.name, which fixes their ownership. Review points: (1) pop() takes from the end, so output order is reversed and depends on traversal; check whether callers rely on order. (2) The qualified name is built from the already-qualified parent, so deep nesting is correct. (3) Methods are re-queued with the qualified classname, but their own closures are processed when they are popped. Confirm their names also get the class prefix, because the method's name is not changed here. (4) Methods pushed from the top-level blocks are not re-owned, so only inner-class methods are adjusted. radon/visitors.py:274-331 builds the closures and inner_classes lists. Closures are collected from nested visitor.functions, and complexity excludes closures (see #68). Inner classes are collected from visitor.classes. Verify the fields in the namedtuples at visitors.py:24-36 line up with what _replace expects, and that methods inside inner classes keep a correct classname before the rewrite. The existing tests in test_complexity_visitor.py:708 cover closure names and complexity but not nested inner-class methods, so a test for that case would be worth adding.

79	    '''Process a list of blocks by adding all closures and inner classes as
80	    top-level blocks.
81	    '''
82	    new_blocks = []
83	    all_blocks = blocks[:]
84	    while all_blocks:

86	        new_blocks.append(block)
87	        for inner_block in ('closures', 'inner_classes'):

92	                    m_named = meth._replace(classname=named.name)
